strengths: REASONMAP targets a useful computer vision problem: interpreting dense transit diagrams while combining station recognition, line tracing, transfer selection, and intermediate-stop reasoning. Its high-resolution real-world maps complement benchmarks centered on abstract puzzles or mathematical reasoning.

The dataset construction includes meaningful quality controls: manually corrected map metadata, human-verified answers, multiple reference routes, and removal of routes that cannot be traced on the supplied maps. Coverage of 30 cities, 13 countries, and four station-name languages provides useful diversity.

The evaluation covers 15 models and exposes substantial remaining difficulty. Table 2 reports best weighted accuracies of 63.02% for short questions and 59.11% for long questions, leaving considerable room for improvement.

The text-only ablation provides evidence that images contribute useful information for several models. For example, Doubao-415 loses 21.61 and 28.90 percentage points on short and long questions, respectively. The qualitative examples also usefully distinguish visual confusion, formatting failures, and refusals.
weaknesses: The correctness metric does not validate the defining requirements of long questions. Algorithm 1 checks line membership, segment endpoints, and transfer continuity, but never checks intermediate-stop identities, their order, or their counts. Consequently, an answer with entirely incorrect intermediate stops can receive full long-question accuracy and the correctness bonus. This materially weakens the interpretation of the reported accuracy as fine-grained reasoning correctness.

The proposed map score is insufficiently justified as a measure of route efficiency or answer quality. It rewards reference-segment matches without defining an optimization objective or directly penalizing unnecessary transfers or distance. It also depends on reference-route length: an exact one-segment short answer receives 15 points, whereas an exact two-segment answer receives 19. Segment alignment for routes of different lengths is unspecified, and the count and IoU formulas have undefined zero-denominator cases. These issues affect the central evaluation contribution, beyond presentation.

The headline comparison between base and reasoning models is confounded by inference settings. Open-source models receive a 2,048-token output limit, while closed-source models use API defaults; some closed-source reasoning models average more than 2,048 tokens on long questions. No truncation rates or token-budget sensitivity experiments are reported. Strict parsing additionally assigns zero to otherwise correct routes with formatting errors, as Figure 5 explicitly illustrates, without quantifying how much this drives the rankings.

The claimed reversal between open- and closed-source reasoning models is broader than the evidence supports. Most comparisons are between different models rather than controlled base/reasoning variants, and Table 2 contains exceptions: Doubao-428 slightly underperforms Doubao-115 on long questions, while Gemini-2.5-Flash trails GPT-4o substantially there. Explanations involving RL-constrained exploration or better visual integration remain hypotheses rather than established findings.

The experimental analysis does not adequately separate visual perception from route reasoning. Removing the image establishes that visual input can help, but there is no map-metadata input baseline or resolution experiment to identify whether failures arise from reading small labels, image preprocessing, or graph reasoning. Appendix D describes general preprocessing strategies without reporting the effective resolutions, tile counts, or visual-token limits used in these experiments.

Reproducibility and statistical support are incomplete. Evaluation uses 312 examples from 11 cities, including only 23 hard questions and a difficulty bucket containing one example, without uncertainty estimates. Manual map-difficulty criteria, annotation agreement, and train/test map overlap are not specified. The manuscript supplies templates and pseudocode, but its Dataset & Toolkit heading has no accessible link, and exact model/API versions and preprocessing configurations are incompletely documented. The benchmark has worthwhile potential, but the metric-validity and comparison-design concerns currently outweigh its supported contribution.

strengths: REASONMAP targets a relevant vision-language problem: extracting connectivity and planning routes from dense, high-resolution transit maps. The combination of text recognition, line tracing, transfers, and intermediate-stop identification offers a useful setting beyond conventional image question answering.

The dataset construction includes meaningful curation: 1,008 route instances across 30 cities, manually corrected map metadata, and verification that reference routes are visible on the maps. Checking feasibility against metadata rather than requiring exact reference-route agreement is a sensible design choice.

The evaluation covers 15 models, includes difficulty and city breakdowns, and provides informative failure examples. The image-removal experiments support the narrower conclusion that visual input improves performance for several tested models: Doubao-415 long-question accuracy drops from 46.09% to 17.19%.
weaknesses: The correctness metric does not validate the central fine-grained requirements. Algorithm 1 checks endpoints, line membership, and transfer continuity but ignores intermediate-stop names and counts, even for long questions. Consequently, a response with completely incorrect intermediate details can receive full accuracy and the correctness bonus in the map score. This separation is disclosed, but it substantially limits what the reported long-question accuracy establishes about fine-grained visual reasoning.

The proposed map score is insufficiently justified as a measure of route quality or efficiency. Algorithm 2 rewards reference-segment overlap without directly measuring excess stops, transfers, or another defined optimization objective. Its unnormalized accumulation also gives different scores to equally perfect answers: an exact one-segment short answer receives 15 points, whereas an exact three-segment answer reaches 20. Set-based intermediate-stop overlap ignores ordering. Segment alignment for routes of different lengths and zero-denominator handling are unspecified. These are substantive metric-validity concerns, beyond the confusing slash notation in the pseudocode.

The headline comparison between base and reasoning models is confounded by inference settings. Open-source models receive only 2,048 output tokens, while closed-source models use API defaults; some closed-source average outputs already exceed that limit. There is no budget sweep or report of truncation rates. Most comparisons also involve different model families or versions rather than matched reasoning configurations. Table 2 contains exceptions to the claimed closed-source trend: Gemini's long-question accuracy is below GPT-4o's, and Doubao-428 is slightly below Doubao-115. The results establish performance under the chosen settings, but not a general reversal in the benefit of reasoning.

Formatting failures are counted as zero performance, and Figure 5 explicitly shows answers containing correct route information rejected for formatting. Without reporting invalid-output rates or a semantic parsing audit, the study cannot determine how much of the ranking reflects map understanding versus output-format compliance. This particularly complicates the interpretation of reasoning-model failures.

The diagnostic evidence does not isolate perception from route reasoning or memorized knowledge. Image removal is useful, but can also trigger refusals, as the appendix acknowledges. No metadata-input baseline or controlled map perturbation separates topology reasoning from visual extraction and prior knowledge. Claims about reinforcement learning restricting exploration, city prominence, and better visual integration therefore remain hypotheses rather than findings established by these experiments.

Reproducibility and uncertainty reporting are incomplete. The evaluation uses 312 instances from 11 maps, with only 23 hard questions and one difficulty bucket containing a single example, yet reports no uncertainty estimates. Exact image-resolution/token limits, API snapshots, parsing normalization, annotation agreement, and train/test map overlap are insufficiently specified. Appendix D describes preprocessing approaches but does not document the actual effective visual inputs. These limitations matter for a benchmark whose principal contribution is trustworthy model comparison. Overall, the worthwhile task and curation do not outweigh the current scoring and experimental-control concerns, supporting weak rejection.

strengths: REASONMAP addresses a useful computer-vision problem: reading dense, high-resolution transit diagrams and composing routes. Its combination of text recognition, line tracing, and connectivity reasoning provides a meaningful evaluation setting.

The dataset includes 1,008 route problems across 30 cities and four station-name languages. Manual correction of map metadata and removal of reference routes that cannot be traced visually are valuable quality-control measures.

The evaluation covers multiple model families, sizes, and question formats. Table 3 provides concrete evidence that images help several models: removing images reduces Doubao-415's weighted accuracy by 21.61 percentage points on short questions and 28.90 points on long questions.

Separating route feasibility from answer quality is conceptually useful, and the supplied templates, evaluation pseudocode, map sources, and qualitative failure examples help readers understand the benchmark.
weaknesses: The correctness metric does not establish correctness of the fine-grained answers. Algorithm 1 checks line membership, segment endpoints, and transfer continuity, but ignores intermediate-stop names, their order, and their counts, even for long questions. Consequently, a response with entirely incorrect intermediate information can receive full accuracy and the correctness bonus. This materially limits interpretation of the headline long-question results.

The proposed map score is not adequately justified as a measure of route efficiency. Algorithm 2 primarily rewards reference agreement and accumulates points without normalization by segment count: an exact one-segment short answer scores 15, while an exact two-segment answer scores 19. It contains no explicit excess-distance or transfer penalty. Segment alignment for unequal-length routes is unspecified, and zero-stop cases can produce undefined divisions. No validation against human quality judgments or graph-based optimality is reported.

The central base-versus-reasoning conclusion is confounded by inference settings and model selection. Open-source models receive only 2,048 output tokens, whereas closed-source models use their API defaults; Table 2 reports an average of 2,372 tokens for o3 on long questions. Truncation rates and token-budget sensitivity are not evaluated. Strict parsing also assigns zero to substantively correct but differently formatted answers, as Figure 5 illustrates. These factors prevent attributing the observed gaps confidently to reasoning capability or RL training.

The claimed reversal for closed-source reasoning models is not consistent across the reported results. Gemini-2.5-Flash obtains 29.86% long-question accuracy versus GPT-4o's 42.80%, and Doubao-428 slightly trails Doubao-115 on that metric. Most comparisons do not isolate reasoning training within a matched model pair; explanations involving knowledge coverage and visual integration remain hypotheses.

Evaluation uncertainty and reproducibility remain insufficiently characterized. Experiments use 312 problems from 11 cities, with only 23 hard questions and one example in the hard-question/medium-map bucket, yet report no confidence intervals or repeated-run variability. Appendix D describes preprocessing architectures but omits actual image-resolution or tile limits used in the experiments. These issues are secondary to the metric and comparison concerns, which determine my weak-reject recommendation despite the dataset's practical promise.

strengths: REASONMAP targets a useful computer-vision problem: interpreting dense, high-resolution transit diagrams and planning routes. Its 30 maps across 13 countries provide realistic variation in layout, language, and network complexity.

The construction pipeline combines structured map extraction, external route references, and manual verification. Appendix A.3 reports review by three domain experts and correction of an initially identified approximately 16% error rate. The city-disjoint training/test setting is a valuable design choice.

Evaluation covers 16 models, with visual-input removal and symbolic-map controls. The substantial improvements from visual maps to symbolic representations—for example, GPT-4o short-question accuracy rising from 41.15% to 82.38%—provide useful evidence of a significant visual-processing bottleneck.

The training baseline demonstrates potential usefulness beyond evaluation. Qwen2.5-VL-7B improves from 13.28% to 26.22% short-question accuracy and from 7.12% to 26.04% long-question accuracy on unseen cities, under the proposed evaluator.
weaknesses: The main concern is evaluator validity. Algorithm 1 checks endpoints, line membership, and transfer continuity, but never checks intermediate-stop lists or counts. Thus, long answers with entirely incorrect requested details can receive full accuracy and the 20-point correctness bonus. Accuracy also does not check optimality despite every template requesting an optimal route. These are material mismatches between the task and its principal metric.

The map score does not establish route efficiency: it rewards reference overlap without directly measuring excess transfers or stops, and accumulated segment points depend on route length. Alternative valid routes can lose points because they differ from the collected references. Algorithm 2 also leaves segment alignment unspecified and divides by zero when both stop counts are zero or both via-stop sets are empty. Table A4 tests weighting variants, but does not validate agreement with actual route quality or resolve these cases.

The headline reasoning-versus-base conclusion is insufficiently controlled. Most comparisons do not isolate reasoning tuning within an otherwise matched model. Open models receive a 2,048-token output limit, whereas closed models use API defaults; no truncation rates or budget-sensitivity results substantiate the assertion that this limit covers complete reasoning generations. The claimed consistent closed-model advantage also has exceptions: Gemini's long accuracy is 29.86%, below GPT-4o's 42.80%.

Format compliance is conflated with reasoning ability. Figure 3 explicitly includes substantively correct route information rejected for formatting, yet the paper does not quantify this contribution to model rankings. Because RL rewards both formatting and endpoint/line correctness, its gains cannot establish improved fine-grained reasoning without separate format-error rates or a supervised/format-only baseline. The claim that non-differentiable evaluation makes SFT insufficient is not technically justified.

The attribution of failures primarily to grounding and spatial reasoning exceeds the evidence. External OCRBench scores and selected examples do not establish how often OCR fails on these particular maps. Appendix B.2 describes general architectures rather than the actual image sizes, tile limits, and visual-token budgets used, leaving perception-related comparison confounds unresolved.

Statistical and implementation support remain incomplete: the test set contains 312 cases from only 11 maps, including just 23 hard questions, without uncertainty estimates. Training duration and reward coefficients are unspecified, and Appendix B.4's stated GRPO objective omits standard normalization/clipping and the KL term mentioned in the setup. Overall, the dataset has worthwhile potential, but the central measurement and comparison issues currently outweigh the acceptance case.

strengths: REASONMAP targets a useful computer vision problem: combining text recognition, visual grounding, and route planning in dense transit diagrams. Its 1,008 paired short/long examples across 30 cities and 13 countries provide a potentially valuable resource beyond conventional visual question answering.

Dataset construction includes manual correction of extracted transit structures and reference routes. Appendix A.3 reports review by three domain experts and correction of approximately 16% initially erroneous examples, demonstrating meaningful quality-control effort.

The evaluation covers 16 models and includes image-removal, symbolic-input, language, and scoring-sensitivity experiments. The visual-input benefit is substantial for several models: Doubao-415 loses 21.61 and 28.90 percentage points on short and long questions when images are removed.

The stated city-disjoint training evaluation is valuable. Reinforcement fine-tuning improves Qwen2.5-VL-7B from 13.28% to 26.22% short-question accuracy and from 7.12% to 26.04% long-question accuracy, establishing a useful baseline under the proposed metrics.
weaknesses: The primary correctness metric does not validate complete answers. Section 4.1 and Algorithm 1 apply the same endpoint, line-membership, and transfer checks to short and long questions, without checking intermediate-stop counts or enumerations. Thus, a long answer with incorrect intermediate stops can receive full accuracy and the additional 20-point correctness bonus. This materially weakens claims about fine-grained reasoning and also affects the RL accuracy reward.

The map score does not adequately establish route efficiency or optimality, although every template requests an optimal route. Algorithm 2 measures overlap with service-provided references without defining an optimization objective, and accumulates segment rewards without normalization by reference length. A perfectly matched one-segment short route scores 15, whereas a perfectly matched two-segment route scores 19. Valid alternative routes can receive lower scores without being less efficient. Set-based stop overlap also ignores order. The limited weighting ablation does not validate these design choices against independently assessed route quality.

The headline conclusion about reasoning models is insufficiently controlled. Most comparisons involve different model families or generations rather than matched base/reasoning variants. Open models have a 2,048-token output cap, whereas closed models use API defaults; no truncation rates or budget-sensitivity results establish that this is harmless. Moreover, the claimed consistently better closed-source reasoning performance has exceptions: Gemini-2.5-Flash reaches 29.86% long accuracy versus GPT-4o's 42.80%, and Doubao-428 slightly trails Doubao-115 on long questions.

Formatting and perception confounds limit the interpretation of low accuracy. Figure 3 explicitly shows correct route information rejected for formatting, but the paper does not quantify how much of each model's deficit comes from parsing rather than visual reasoning. Appendix B.2 describes model architectures without reporting the actual image resolutions, tile counts, or visual-token budgets used. These settings are particularly consequential for maps averaging 5,839 × 5,449 pixels.

The training experiment demonstrates improvement under the evaluator, but does not isolate improved visual reasoning from improved output formatting. There is no format-only reward ablation or supervised fine-tuning comparison. Section 4.3's assertion that SFT is insufficient because the metrics are non-differentiable is not justified: supervised learning can improve those outcomes without differentiating through the evaluation metric. Appendix B.4 also omits reward magnitudes, training duration, and important details connecting its simplified policy-gradient objective to the stated GRPO implementation.

The benchmark has only 312 test examples across 11 maps, including 23 hard questions and one difficulty bucket containing a single example. No uncertainty estimates accompany model comparisons. This does not invalidate the resource, but limits broad conclusions about reasoning behavior; selected failure cases and external OCRBench scores do not establish that grounding and spatial reasoning are the principal causes of the observed performance gap. Overall, the resource has worthwhile merits, but the mismatch between task requirements and evaluation, together with insufficiently controlled central claims, makes the present balance favor rejection.

strengths: REASONMAP targets a useful computer-vision problem: interpreting dense transit maps requires reading station labels, grounding them to lines, and planning routes. The combination is a worthwhile benchmark contribution.

The dataset includes 1,008 route problems across 30 cities and 13 countries, with short and detailed answer variants. Manual correction of extracted topology and review by three domain experts provide meaningful quality control (Section 3 and Appendix A.3).

The evaluation covers 16 MLLMs and includes informative visual-input removal, symbolic-input, difficulty, and city analyses. For example, Doubao-415 short-question accuracy falls from 43.14% with maps to 21.53% without them, supporting the usefulness of visual information.

The city-disjoint training evaluation is valuable. Reinforcement fine-tuning improves Qwen2.5-VL-7B short/long accuracy from 13.28%/7.12% to 26.22%/26.04%, demonstrating that the dataset can support learning beyond the training cities.
weaknesses: The principal concern is evaluation validity. Algorithm 1 checks line membership, segment endpoints, and transfer continuity, but never checks the intermediate-stop counts or lists requested by long questions. Thus, an answer with entirely incorrect intermediate stops can receive full long-question accuracy and the 20-point correctness bonus. This also affects the RL accuracy reward and materially weakens claims about improving fine-grained reasoning.

The map score does not establish the claimed measurement of route efficiency. Prompts request an optimal route, but optimality is not formally defined, and Algorithm 2 rewards reference overlap rather than excess stops, transfers, or travel cost. Its set-based intermediate-stop comparison ignores order. Consequently, the separate quality metric does not fully resolve the limitations of the correctness metric.

The headline conclusion about reasoning models is stronger than the comparisons support. Most models are not controlled base/reasoning pairs, and the claimed consistently stronger closed-source reasoning performance has exceptions: Gemini-2.5-Flash achieves 29.86% long accuracy versus GPT-4o's 42.80%, while Doubao-428 slightly trails Doubao-115 on long questions. Selected reasoning traces do not establish stronger visual grounding as the primary cause of the observed differences.

Inference and training details leave consequential reproducibility gaps. Appendix B.2 describes architectural image-processing strategies but does not report the actual image-resolution or visual-token limits used. The 2,048-token generation limit for open models lacks a truncation audit. Appendix B.4 provides a simplified policy-gradient objective without specifying the complete GRPO implementation, reward coefficients, or training duration.

The training results do not distinguish improved route reasoning from improved format compliance, although format failures are explicitly documented and format reward is part of training. No format-only or SFT comparison is supplied; the assertion that nondifferentiable evaluation metrics make SFT insufficient is not technically justified.

Statistical support is limited for fine-grained conclusions: the test set contains 312 problems from 11 maps, with only 23 hard questions and one sample in one difficulty bucket. No uncertainty estimates are reported. Overall, the dataset has worthwhile merits, but the central scoring mismatch and insufficiently controlled interpretations currently favor rejection; these concerns are more consequential than presentation refinements.
